360-chicago.text: The observatory floor sits 1,030 feet above the street in the tower long known as the John Hancock Center. Independently run and rebranded 360 Chicago in 2014, it added TILT that same summer — floor-to-ceiling windows that slowly tilt visitors out to 30 degrees over the street — alongside an open-air SkyWalk and the CloudBar cocktail lounge.
360-chicago.descriptor: 94th-floor observation deck in the former John Hancock Center

abraham-lincoln-the-man.text: Augustus Saint-Gaudens's 12-foot bronze, finished in 1887 and known everywhere as the Standing Lincoln, shows Lincoln rising from a chair of state to speak; Stanford White designed the pedestal and exedra around it in Lincoln Park. Chicago businessman Eli Bates left $40,000 for the statue, and Saint-Gaudens worked from a life mask and hand casts taken of Lincoln in 1860. Recasts stand in London and Mexico City.
abraham-lincoln-the-man.descriptor: Saint-Gaudens's 1887 'Standing Lincoln' bronze in Lincoln Park

al-capones-house.text: Al Capone moved into this Park Manor two-flat at 7244 S. Prairie Ave. on August 8, 1923 — a six-bedroom, two-story building put up in 1905 on a 68-foot-wide double lot, bought for $5,500. It was his Chicago home in the years he built up the city's Prohibition rackets, and it is an ordinary South Side brick house rather than a gangster's mansion.
al-capones-house.descriptor: Al Capone's 1920s family two-flat on S Prairie Ave in Park Manor

albert-ivar-goodman-theatre.text: The Goodman was founded in 1925 as a memorial to playwright Kenneth Sawyer Goodman, who died in the 1918 flu pandemic, and won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 1992. It moved in 2000 to 170 N. Dearborn, where its two auditoriums — the Albert and the Owen — sit inside the landmarked 1922 Harris and Selwyn theaters, gutted and rebuilt behind their preserved facades.
albert-ivar-goodman-theatre.descriptor: Goodman Theatre mainstage at 170 N Dearborn in the Loop theater district

alinea.text: Opened in 2005 by chef Grant Achatz and Nick Kokonas, Alinea built its name on theatrical, maximalist modernist cooking. It won the James Beard award for Outstanding Restaurant in 2016 and held three Michelin stars from 2011 until it was cut to two in November 2025.
alinea.descriptor: Grant Achatz's modernist tasting-menu restaurant on N Halsted, Lincoln Park

als-beef.text: Al's has been making Italian beef since 1938, when Al Ferreri started it with his sister Frances and brother-in-law Chris Pacelli Sr.; a grandson of the founder still runs the company, which operates a Taylor Street shop in Little Italy. The sandwich is the Chicago template: heavily seasoned roast beef in gravy on soft French bread with sweet or hot peppers.
als-beef.descriptor: Italian beef stand on Taylor Street in Little Italy

als-beef-river-north.text: Al's has been making Italian beef since 1938, when Al Ferreri started it with his sister Frances and brother-in-law Chris Pacelli Sr.; the Taylor Street shop in Little Italy is the chain's original location, and a grandson of the founder still runs the company. The sandwich is the Chicago template: heavily seasoned roast beef in gravy on soft French bread with sweet peppers or hot giardiniera.
als-beef-river-north.descriptor: Original 1938 Italian beef stand on Taylor Street in Little Italy

ann-sather-restaurant.text: Ann Sather, the Swedish immigrant who ran this Lakeview diner, was retiring and closing up in 1981 when a young Tom Tunney talked her into selling it to him instead. He grew it into a small local chain and later spent two decades as 44th Ward alderman. The oversized cinnamon rolls that come with almost every order are what people actually come for.
ann-sather-restaurant.descriptor: Swedish-American diner on W Belmont known for giant cinnamon rolls

apollo-theater.text: The Apollo is the off-Loop commercial house at 2550 N Lincoln Ave where "Million Dollar Quartet" moved in on October 31, 2008 and stayed until January 17, 2016 — a run of more than seven years, the third-longest-running show by calendar span in Chicago theater history. It still books open-ended commercial productions and touring shows.
apollo-theater.descriptor: Off-Loop commercial theater at 2550 N Lincoln Ave in Lincoln Park

arie-crown-theater.text: The theater is named for Arie Crown, the Lithuanian immigrant father of industrialist Henry Crown, and opened in 1960 with 5,000 seats — one of the largest houses in Chicago. A 1967 fire shut it until 1971, and later acoustic work reshaped the hall down to 4,188 seats. Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, the Rolling Stones, David Bowie and Aretha Franklin have all played it.

art-of-pizza.text: The Art of Pizza has served the Lakeview area for more than 30 years and sells its deep dish both by the whole pie and by the slice, in thin-crust and pan-stuffed styles. The restaurant cites a Chicago Tribune ranking that put its deep dish first, with judges praising a "near-perfect, golden-brown crust" and a sauce with "nice, herby flavors."
art-of-pizza.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish and stuffed pizza sold by the slice

au-cheval.text: Hogsalt's Au Cheval opened in 2012 at 800 W. Randolph in the West Loop, a compact all-day diner with counter and booth seating. Its cheeseburger — American cheese, dijonnaise, pickles, grilled onions — is called by many the best in Chicago, and the room is notoriously hard to get into: once the text says your table is ready, you have ten minutes to claim it.
au-cheval.descriptor: West Loop diner on W Randolph known for its cheeseburger, since 2012

auditorium-theatre.text: Adler and Sullivan's 1889 masterpiece was dedicated by President Benjamin Harrison on December 9, 1889, with opera star Adelina Patti singing that night. It was among the first buildings lit entirely by incandescent bulbs and carried one of the earliest central air-conditioning systems, and it was the first home of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. Roosevelt University has occupied the building since 1946.
auditorium-theatre.descriptor: 1889 Adler & Sullivan theater on Michigan Ave, inside Roosevelt University

avec.text: One Off Hospitality's second restaurant started life as a wine bar and made its name as much on the room as the food — it won a James Beard Award for Outstanding Restaurant Design in 2005. Chef and co-founder Paul Kahan took Beard's Best Chef: Great Lakes in 2004 and Outstanding Chef in 2013.
avec.descriptor: Mediterranean small plates and wine bar on West Randolph's restaurant row

batter-berries.text: Craig and Tanya Richardson opened Batter & Berries on North Lincoln Avenue in 2012, and the Black-owned brunch room made its name on the French toast flight — a sampler of thin, eggy slices in rotating flavors served with housemade maple butter. The other signature is the Cluk-N-Gaufre: pulled chicken in a sweet-potato waffle with a fried chicken breast on top.
batter-berries.descriptor: Lincoln Park brunch spot on N Lincoln Ave known for its French toast flight

bavettes-bar-boeuf.text: Bavette's is Hogsalt's steakhouse at 218 W. Kinzie in River North, done up in jazz-era decor with music to match. Steak frites is the headline, but Time Out's line is that the fried and roasted chicken rival the beef, and the pies — lemon meringue, chocolate cream — have their own following. Reservations open 21 days ahead at 9am; walk-ins may have better odds.
bavettes-bar-boeuf.descriptor: Jazz-era steakhouse at 218 W Kinzie in River North

beatrix-streeterville.text: Beatrix is Lettuce Entertain You's all-day "healthy meets delicious" concept — from Rich Melman and Marc Jacobs with chef partners John Chiakulas, Rita Dever and Susan Weaver — that works as coffeehouse, bakery and restaurant at once, with Beatrix Coffee Roasters at the coffee bar. The house-baked cookies are what people walk out with.
beatrix-streeterville.descriptor: Lettuce Entertain You all-day cafe and bakery on N. St. Clair

begin-route-66.text: This is the eastern end of Route 66: the "Begin Historic Illinois U.S. Route 66" markers stand on Adams Street at Michigan Avenue, where westbound drivers start the drive. The 1926 route actually began a block south at Jackson Boulevard; when Jackson became one-way eastbound in 1955 the westbound traffic was shifted north to Adams, which is why the "End" signs are still on Jackson.
begin-route-66.descriptor: "Begin Historic Route 66" sign on Adams St at Michigan Ave

belmont-harbor.text: Belmont Harbor provides about 730 moorings along with a fuel dock and a ship store, and the Chicago Yacht Club keeps a Belmont station here. Just inland is the Bill Jarvis Migratory Bird Sanctuary, first landscaped in the 1920s and nearly bulldozed for a golf course in 1968 until Lake View neighbors — including Bill Jarvis — led a successful campaign to save it; it now hosts more than 150 bird species.
belmont-harbor.descriptor: Lakefront marina with 730 moorings, in Lincoln Park off Addison St

berlin-wall-monument.text: A real section of the Berlin Wall stands inside the CTA's Western Brown Line station. The German government offered Chicago the piece in 2008, dedicated to the city's residents for helping "secure the freedom" of Berlin, and the city installed it in Lincoln Square — historically its most German-American neighborhood.
berlin-wall-monument.descriptor: Berlin Wall slab inside the Western Brown Line station, Lincoln Square

big-chicks.text: Michelle Fire opened Big Chicks on December 11, 1986 in what had been a veterans' bar, inheriting the old regulars and the bartenders along with the room. It has since become an informal gay community center for Uptown, hung with her own art collection, and was inducted into the Chicago LGBT Hall of Fame in 2016.
big-chicks.descriptor: Uptown gay bar open since 1986, hung with the owner's art collection

big-jones.text: Paul Fehribach and Mark Armantrout opened Big Jones in 2008 to cook regional Southern food out of the archives — antebellum heirloom grits, house charcuterie, revived historic dishes — sourced from local farms and Southern artisan producers. Fehribach is an eight-time James Beard Award semifinalist for Best Chef: Great Lakes and has written two books on the history of Southern cooking.
big-jones.descriptor: Heirloom Southern cooking on N Clark St in Andersonville since 2008

big-star.text: Big Star is a honky-tonk taqueria modeled on the bars of Bakersfield, California, with executive chef-partner Paul Kahan behind the food: house-made tortillas, tacos al pastor, Baja and panza, a soundtrack running classic country to '70s rock, and 20 exclusive house-barrel bourbons out of Kentucky. It spun off its own label, Big Star Recording Co., in 2016.
big-star.descriptor: Honky-tonk taqueria and bourbon bar at 1531 N Damen in Wicker Park

big-star-west-town.text: Big Star is the taco-and-whiskey bar from One Off Hospitality, the group behind The Publican, avec and The Violet Hour, whose partners Paul Kahan and Donnie Madia both hold James Beard awards. It serves a short menu of tacos, whiskey and beer in a lively, no-frills room, and has two Chicago locations: Wicker Park and Wrigleyville.
big-star-west-town.descriptor: Taco, whiskey and beer bar from One Off Hospitality

billy-goat-tavern.text: William "Billy Goat" Sianis opened his first tavern in 1934 and moved the business below street level at 430 N. Michigan in 1964, near the Tribune and Sun-Times offices. He is the source of the Curse of the Billy Goat: ejected with his pet goat from Game 4 of the 1945 World Series at Wrigley, he cursed the Cubs — who won no title until 2016.
billy-goat-tavern.descriptor: Below-street burger tavern on Lower Michigan Ave since 1964

biograph-theatre.text: On July 22, 1934, John Dillinger walked out of the Biograph after a movie and was shot dead on the sidewalk by FBI agents led by Melvin Purvis. Designed by Samuel N. Crowen in 1914 in red pressed brick and white-glazed terra cotta, it is on the National Register (1984) and was made a Chicago Landmark in 2001; Victory Gardens Theater bought it in 2004 and reopened it as a live stage in 2006.
biograph-theatre.descriptor: 1914 movie house on Lincoln Ave, now Victory Gardens Theater

birrieria-zaragoza.text: Birrieria Zaragoza built its reputation on one dish: slow-cooked goat that never touches the consommé until it is plated, when some of the tomato-based broth is spooned over it. The family-owned original stands at 4852 S Pulaski Rd in Archer Heights; a second location opened in Uptown at 4800 N Broadway in 2023.
birrieria-zaragoza.descriptor: Family-run goat birria specialist on S Pulaski Rd in Archer Heights

bloomingdale-trail-park.text: The 606 runs on the Bloomingdale Line, a freight track built in 1873 by the Chicago & Pacific Railroad; the city bought the right-of-way from Canadian Pacific in January 2013 and opened the park on June 6, 2015. At 2.7 miles it's the longest elevated rail-to-trail greenway in the Western Hemisphere — and the name is an homage to 606, the prefix of nearly every Chicago ZIP code.
bloomingdale-trail-park.descriptor: The 606: 2.7-mile elevated rail-trail park above Bloomingdale Ave

blue-chicago.text: The building opened in the early 1970s as a dive country bar on a former used-car lot, drawing cops and neighborhood regulars, and reopened as Bluelight in September 2006 under the owners of Rebel Bar & Grill and Pitchfork. The blue neon marquee still advertises the draw — "the light is on til 4am" — and the house pour is the Bluelight Special: vodka, blue curaçao and pineapple in a 32-ounce mug.
blue-chicago.descriptor: Late-night dive bar on N Western Ave in Roscoe Village with a 4 a.m. license

blues-heaven-garden.text: The garden sits beside 2120 S. Michigan Ave., the Chess Records studio where Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley recorded from 1957 to 1967, and where the Rolling Stones cut an instrumental named for the address in 1964. Willie Dixon's widow Marie bought the building — a Chicago Landmark since 1990 — in 1993 and opened it as Blues Heaven in 1997; the foundation has run free Record Row concerts in the garden for more than two decades.
blues-heaven-garden.descriptor: Outdoor concert garden beside the old Chess Records studio on S. Michigan

boka.text: Boka opened in 2003 and became the seed of the Boka Restaurant Group, now one of Chicago's biggest restaurant families. Chef partner Lee Wolen took over the kitchen in 2014; the restaurant held a Michelin star every year from 2011 through 2025, and Wolen has collected multiple James Beard nominations and the Chicago Tribune's 2015 Chef of the Year.
boka.descriptor: Seasonal American fine dining from Boka Restaurant Group, open since 2003

buckingham-fountain.text: Kate Sturges Buckingham gave the fountain to Chicago in 1927 as a memorial to her brother Clarence. Architect Edward H. Bennett modeled it on the Latona Fountain at Versailles, and its four sets of seahorses stand for the states bordering Lake Michigan: Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Wisconsin. The center jet throws water 150 feet, and the fountain opened Married... with Children.
buckingham-fountain.descriptor: Rococo fountain in Grant Park with a 150-foot center jet, given in 1927

buona.text: This Roosevelt Road stand is where Buona began: in 1981 Joe and Peggy Buonavolanto took a $10,000 second mortgage on their house half a mile away to open it. Peggy worked out the Italian beef recipe with help from her uncle "Junior," who ran Mr. Beef on Orleans Street. Their five sons grew it into the country's largest family-owned Italian beef group.
buona.descriptor: The original 1981 Buona Italian beef stand on Roosevelt Rd in Berwyn

burnham-park.text: Burnham Park is the 598-acre, six-mile lakefront strip built largely on landfill and named in 1927 for Daniel Burnham, whose 1909 Plan of Chicago called for it. It hosted the 1933–34 Century of Progress world's fair, and its landforms include Northerly Island — the only offshore island in the Burnham Plan that actually got built — plus Promontory Point and 31st Street Beach.
burnham-park.descriptor: Six-mile lakefront park on landfill, Grant Park down to Jackson Park

butch-mcguires.text: Butch McGuire borrowed money from his mother to open on Division Street in 1961 and became known as the unofficial mayor of the strip. The bar's own history calls it a premier singles bar and claims more than 10,000 marriages have come out of encounters there. Every winter it disappears under holiday decorations and double-decker model trains, with proceeds going to Mercy Home.
butch-mcguires.descriptor: Gold Coast saloon on Division Street since 1961, famed for Christmas decor

byline-bank-aragon-ballroom.text: Opened July 15, 1926, the Aragon was given an interior by theater architect John Eberson evoking the courtyard of a Moorish castle around a 21,000-square-foot dance floor. In its heyday crowds topping 18,000 a week danced here to nightly WGN broadcasts heard across the U.S., Canada and reportedly Britain; it's now a 5,000-capacity Live Nation venue, known as the Byline Bank Aragon since 2019.
byline-bank-aragon-ballroom.descriptor: 1926 Moorish-castle ballroom and concert hall in Uptown

cadillac-palace-theatre.text: It opened on Randolph Street in 1926 as the New Palace, a French Baroque vaudeville house designed by Rapp and Rapp. Its brass ornament was painted white during World War II so the government wouldn't requisition the metal; a $20 million restoration in 1999 uncovered it again. The 2,344-seat house now takes pre-Broadway tryouts, among them The Producers in 2001.
cadillac-palace-theatre.descriptor: 1926 Rapp & Rapp Loop theater on W. Randolph, now a Broadway touring house

cafe-ba-ba-reeba.text: Cafe Ba-Ba-Reeba! opened at 2024 N. Halsted in 1985 as Chicago's original tapas bar, a Lettuce Entertain You restaurant that introduced the city to small plates and pitchers of sangria. Four decades on it's still known for paella, croquetas and bacon-wrapped dates.
cafe-ba-ba-reeba.descriptor: Spanish tapas and paella on N. Halsted in Lincoln Park since 1985

carmines.text: A Gold Coast fixture on the Rush Street strip, Carmine's belongs to Alex Dana's Rosebud Restaurant Group and trades in old-school Italian — handmade pasta, generous portions built for a table. It reopened in January 2026 after a $4 million rebuild, and added an all-weather second-floor terrace overlooking the Gold Coast that June.
carmines.descriptor: Rush Street Italian restaurant from the Rosebud group, with a second-floor terrace

carousel.text: The carousel turns in Pier Park at Navy Pier alongside the Centennial Wheel, the teacups and the Wave Swinger. The original ride ran from the pier's 1995 reopening until a cold-weather mechanical failure in early 2019; the replacement installed that summer had previously spun at Dorney Park in Pennsylvania.
carousel.descriptor: Carousel ride in Pier Park at Navy Pier

carsons-ribs.text: Dean Carson, a third-generation Chicagoan from a family that had been in food and beverage since the 1930s, opened Carson's in 1977 on a promise of large portions of great food at an honest price, built around baby back ribs in the house barbecue sauce. It still advertises itself as 'America's #1 Barbecue' and has added outposts in Deerfield and Milwaukee.
carsons-ribs.descriptor: Barbecue rib house at 465 E Illinois St in Streeterville, since 1977

centennial-wheel.text: Named for Navy Pier's 100th anniversary, the Centennial Wheel debuted May 27, 2016 to replace the pier's 1995 Ferris wheel — 46 feet taller at 196 feet, with a twelve-minute ride of three full revolutions in enclosed, climate-controlled gondolas. It's a Dutch Wheels DW60, the first of its kind in the United States, built to take 115 mph winds.
centennial-wheel.descriptor: 196-foot Ferris wheel with enclosed gondolas at Navy Pier

ceres-cafe.text: Ceres sits in the lobby of the Chicago Board of Trade Building at 141 W. Jackson and takes its name from the Roman goddess of agriculture whose statue crowns the building. It opened as the Broker's Inn in 1967, took the Ceres name in December 1989, and has been a commodities traders' haunt ever since — famous enough for its punishing pours that it lent its name to a first-season episode of The Bear.
ceres-cafe.descriptor: Bar and diner in the Board of Trade lobby, known for heavy pours

charles-wacker.text: Charles H. Wacker (1856–1929), a brewing and malting executive turned civic booster, chaired the Chicago Plan Commission from 1909 to 1926 and spent those years selling Burnham's Plan of Chicago to the public through speeches, press coverage and Wacker's Manual of the Plan of Chicago. Wacker Drive carries his name, and he's buried here in Graceland, the 1860 cemetery nicknamed the "Cemetery of Architects."
charles-wacker.descriptor: Grave in Graceland Cemetery of the man Wacker Drive is named for

chicago-architecture-center.text: Founded in 1966 as the Chicago School of Architecture Foundation — originally to save H.H. Richardson's Glessner House — it was renamed the Chicago Architecture Foundation in 1979 and moved into Mies van der Rohe's One Illinois Center on the river in 2018. Its centerpiece is the Chicago Model, a 3-D printed scale model of the central city, and it runs the docent-led architecture river cruise and Open House Chicago, the city's largest annual architecture event.
chicago-architecture-center.descriptor: Architecture museum on the Chicago River with a 3-D scale model of the city

chicago-childrens-museum.text: The Junior League of Chicago founded the museum in 1982 in response to programming cutbacks in the Chicago Public Schools, starting it inside the Chicago Public Library. It moved to Navy Pier in 1995, and a 2006 plan to relocate to Grant Park drew neighborhood opposition and was rejected by the Park District in 2011; the museum then signed a 90-year Navy Pier lease in late 2012.
chicago-childrens-museum.descriptor: Hands-on children's museum at Navy Pier since 1995

chicago-cultural-center.text: Built in 1897 as Chicago's central public library and a Grand Army of the Republic memorial hall, the building became the nation's first free municipal cultural center in 1978. Preston Bradley Hall's 38-foot Tiffany glass dome, made of more than 60,000 pieces of glass, is billed as the largest in the world, and there's a second stained-glass dome by Healy and Millet. Admission is still free.
chicago-cultural-center.descriptor: Free city arts venue in the 1897 former public library, 78 E. Washington

chicago-history-museum.text: Founded in 1856 as the Chicago Historical Society, it lost its original collection — including Lincoln's final draft of the Emancipation Proclamation — in the Great Chicago Fire, and adopted its current public name in 2006. Its roughly 22 million holdings include Lincoln's deathbed and the table on which Lee signed his 1865 surrender to Grant.
chicago-history-museum.descriptor: Lincoln Park museum of Chicago history at Clark and North Ave

chicago-pizza-and-oven-grinder-co.text: Open since 1972, it serves a "pizza pot pie" — Sicilian dough baked upside down over sauce and cheese in a bowl, then flipped at your table. The garage across Clark Street was the site of the 1929 St. Valentine's Day Massacre, and legend says this building was a lookout for Capone's gunmen, though there's no evidence for it.
chicago-pizza-and-oven-grinder-co.descriptor: Lincoln Park pizza spot since 1972, known for its upside-down pizza pot pie

writtenFor.name: Chicago Pizza and Oven Grinder Co.

chicago-riverwalk.text: A pedestrian walkway on the south bank of the Chicago River's main branch, begun with the 2001 Wacker Drive reconstruction and expanded in phases through 2016. The expansion laid out six "rooms" — Marina Plaza, the Cove, River Theater, Water Plaza, the Jetty, the Boardwalk — with floating wetland gardens, fishing piers and amphitheater steps down to the water.
chicago-riverwalk.descriptor: Public promenade along the Chicago River's main branch downtown

chicago-shakespeare-theater.text: Barbara Gaines founded the company in 1986 as a workshop staging Shakespeare on the roof of a Lincoln Park pub. It opened its purpose-built Navy Pier home in 1999, built around a 510-seat Courtyard Theater whose thrust stage wraps the audience close on three sides. The company won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 2008 and added The Yard, a reconfigurable 150-to-850-seat space, in 2017.
chicago-shakespeare-theater.descriptor: Navy Pier theater with a courtyard thrust stage, founded 1986

chicago-theatre.text: Rapp & Rapp built it as the flagship of the Balaban & Katz chain, promoted as the "Wonder Theatre of the World"; it opened in 1921 with films, stage shows and a 26-rank Wurlitzer organ, and seats about 3,600. The vertical CHICAGO sign, hung with the Y-shaped municipal device that stands for the forked Chicago River, has become an unofficial emblem of the city.
chicago-theatre.descriptor: 1921 State Street movie palace with the landmark CHICAGO marquee

chicago-union-station.text: Completed in 1925 from a Daniel Burnham plan and finished by Graham, Anderson, Probst & White after his death, its Great Hall sits under a barrel-vaulted skylight 115 feet up. The travertine staircase is where Brian De Palma shot the baby-carriage shootout in The Untouchables (1987).
chicago-union-station.descriptor: 1925 Beaux-Arts rail terminal in the West Loop with a soaring Great Hall

chicago-water-tower.text: Built in 1869 to William W. Boyington's design in yellowing Lemont limestone, it was the only public building in the burned zone to survive the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 — though its roof, not made of limestone, caught fire and the pumps stopped working. It now holds the City Gallery, a free photography space run by the city's tourism office.
chicago-water-tower.descriptor: 1869 limestone tower on Michigan Ave, now a free city art gallery

cho-sun-ok-restaurant.text: Cho Sun Ok has held the corner of Lincoln and Berteau in North Center since 1980. Time Out's advice is to talk the server into letting you cook the sliced beef yourself at the table rather than have it done in the kitchen — it comes out more tender — and to work through the long spread of banchan side dishes.
cho-sun-ok-restaurant.descriptor: Old-school Korean BBQ at Lincoln and Berteau, tabletop grills, since 1980

cibc-theatre.text: It opened in 1906 as the Majestic Theatre, a vaudeville house designed by Edmund R. Krause with the Rapp brothers, running a dozen-plus acts a day. Now an 1,800-seat Broadway In Chicago venue, it has cycled through names — Shubert, LaSalle Bank, Bank of America, PrivateBank, then CIBC in 2017 — and hosted the Chicago sit-down of Hamilton from 2016 to 2020.
cibc-theatre.descriptor: 1,800-seat Loop Broadway house that opened in 1906 as the Majestic Theatre

city-winery.text: Michael Dorf opened the first City Winery in New York in 2008 and brought the format to Chicago's West Loop in 2012: wine actually made and barreled on the premises, a Mediterranean-leaning restaurant, and a ticketed stage running rock, blues, jazz, R&B and comedy.
city-winery.descriptor: Working urban winery and seated concert venue at 1200 W. Randolph

civic-opera-house.text: Utilities magnate Samuel Insull built this 1929 Art Deco house, whose silhouette is seen as a huge chair — earning the nickname "Insull's Throne." It opened on November 4, 1929, days after the stock market crash. The 3,276-seat auditorium has been home to the Lyric Opera of Chicago since 1954, and the Joffrey Ballet since 2021.
civic-opera-house.descriptor: Art Deco opera house at 20 N Wacker, home of the Lyric Opera

coalfire.text: Coalfire's Valoriani brick oven burns clean coal at around 1,500 degrees, turning out blistered, leopard-spotted thin crust in under two minutes. Chicago Magazine voted it the #1 best pizza in Chicago.
coalfire.descriptor: Coal-oven thin-crust pizza at 1321 W. Grand Ave in West Town

columbus-park.text: Jens Jensen began designing Columbus Park in 1915 and it was largely finished by 1920 — the 135-acre Prairie School landscape widely considered his masterwork, with stone waterfalls, a council ring and native plantings that were rare for the time. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2003.
columbus-park.descriptor: Jens Jensen's 135-acre prairie-style park in Austin, with waterfalls and council ring

connies-pizza.text: In 1963 Jim Stolfe traded his Oldsmobile Starfire for a small storefront pizzeria on 26th Street on the South Side. It already carried the previous owner's name, and by the time he could afford to change the sign, Connie's had stuck. The family business later moved to its big Archer Avenue flagship and built a deep-dish empire from there.
connies-pizza.descriptor: Deep-dish pizza institution at 2373 S. Archer Ave on the South Side since 1963

connies-pizza-armour-square.text: Connie's has been making Chicago deep dish on Archer Avenue since 1963. The Near South Side room is built for volume — it seats up to 400, with ample parking — and sits just minutes from the Loop.
connies-pizza-armour-square.descriptor: Deep-dish pizzeria on S. Archer Ave, since 1963

contemporary.text: These galleries sit inside the Art Institute's Modern Wing, the 264,000-square-foot Renzo Piano addition that opened in May 2009 and made the Art Institute the second-largest art museum in the United States after the Met. The wing holds European modernism, art from 1960 onward, photography, design and architecture, and its Nichols Bridgeway carries you from the rooftop sculpture garden into Millennium Park.
contemporary.descriptor: Contemporary art galleries in the Art Institute's Renzo Piano Modern Wing

coq-dor.text: The Drake's lower-level lounge dates to the end of Prohibition — the hotel says Coq d'Or was the second establishment in Chicago to be granted a liquor license once drinking was legal again. It has stayed the same kind of room ever since: small, intimate and sultry, built for live jazz, cocktails and hushed conversation.
coq-dor.descriptor: Wood-paneled piano bar in the lower level of the Drake Hotel

court-theatre.text: Founded in 1955, Court is the University of Chicago's professional theater company, staging four plays a season at 5535 S. Ellis Ave. for more than 35,000 people a year. In 2022 it won the Regional Theatre Tony Award, one of the most prestigious honors for a theater outside New York.
court-theatre.descriptor: Classic-repertory theater on the U. of Chicago campus in Hyde Park

crown-fountain.text: Jaume Plensa's 2004 fountain sets two 50-foot glass-block towers facing each other across a shallow black granite reflecting pool. Each plays video portraits of about 1,000 Chicago residents in random rotation, and water appears to spout from the mouths of the projected faces — a modern take on the gargoyle fountain.
crown-fountain.descriptor: Millennium Park video fountain with 50-foot glass-block towers

cubby-bear.text: Established in 1953 at Addison and Clark across from Wrigley Field, the Cubby Bear is a game-day institution that doubles as a rock club — it built a name on rock and punk bookings, and its stage has hosted Johnny Cash and B.B. King as well as Dave Matthews Band and No Doubt.
cubby-bear.descriptor: Sports bar and rock club across from Wrigley Field since 1953

delilahs.text: A rock-and-roll bar at 2771 N. Lincoln Ave. that pours an enormous whiskey list alongside more than 300 beers, with DJs spinning punk and classic rock Sunday through Thursday and the jukebox in customers' hands on weekends. It is open 365 days a year, and tastings are a regular fixture.
delilahs.descriptor: Rock-and-roll dive bar on N. Lincoln Ave with a huge whiskey list

devil-dawgs-chicago-loop.text: Devil Dawgs started in 2010 in Lincoln Park a few steps from DePaul, following in the footsteps of the iconic Demon Dogs, with the stated aim of bringing the great Chicago-style hot dog and fries back to the neighborhood. It has since grown to seven spots, including this one on Milwaukee Avenue in Wicker Park.
devil-dawgs-chicago-loop.descriptor: Chicago-style hot dogs and burgers on Milwaukee Ave in Wicker Park

doughnut-vault.text: Restaurateur Brendan Sodikoff runs Doughnut Vault out of a chandeliered vestibule that holds roughly four people. It bakes a fixed batch each morning — around 750 doughnuts, buttermilk old-fashioned and chestnut-glazed among them — and shuts the window once they're gone, which is why the line down Franklin Street is part of the ritual.
doughnut-vault.descriptor: Tiny walk-up doughnut window on N Franklin St in River North

duck-duck-goat.text: Stephanie Izard — the first woman to win Top Chef — runs this Chinese-American restaurant, with hand-pulled noodles, house-made dumplings and BBQ ribs in a room styled as an 'everytown Chinatown.' It's her third restaurant with Boka Restaurant Group, after Girl & the Goat, and its signature crab rangoon goes back to a childhood favorite of hers.
duck-duck-goat.descriptor: Stephanie Izard's Chinese-American restaurant in the West Loop

dusable-black-history-museum-and-educati.text: Chartered on February 16, 1961 by Margaret Taylor-Burroughs, her husband Charles and others, it started in their own home as the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art before moving to Washington Park in 1973. It is the nation's oldest museum of African American culture, holds some 13,000 artifacts, and is named for Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, Chicago's first non-Native permanent settler.
dusable-black-history-museum-and-educati.descriptor: Washington Park museum of Black history and culture, founded in 1961

writtenFor.name: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center

ebenezer-missionary-baptist-church.text: Dankmar Adler — Louis Sullivan's partner — designed this Grand Boulevard building in 1899 as the Isaiah Temple synagogue; the Black Ebenezer congregation bought it in 1921 as the neighborhood changed. The first gospel chorus was formed here in 1931 under Thomas A. Dorsey and Theodore Frye, and the church's music nurtured Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin and Dinah Washington.
ebenezer-missionary-baptist-church.descriptor: 1899 Grand Boulevard church built as a synagogue by architect Dankmar Adler

ed-debevics.text: Rich Melman and Lee Cohn opened Ed Debevic's in 1984 around a fictional backstory: Ed, a Korean War vet, ran the joint. The gimmick is servers who insult you and put on choreographed numbers. The original Wells Street building in River North was demolished in 2015, and the diner reopened in Streeterville in 2021.
ed-debevics.descriptor: 1950s-style diner with wisecracking servers on E Ohio St, Streeterville, since 1984

elis-cheesecake.text: Eli Schulman, who ran Eli's The Place for Steak, developed the cream-cheese-and-shortbread recipe in the late 1970s and sold it at the first Taste of Chicago in 1980, where it became the festival's signature dessert. The company moved to this 62,000-square-foot Dunning bakery in 1996 and has baked inaugural cakes for Bill Clinton and Barack Obama.
elis-cheesecake.descriptor: Cheesecake bakery and café in Dunning, on the Northwest Side

emmett-till-mamie-till-mobley-house.text: This brick two-flat in West Woodlawn was home to Emmett Till and his mother Mamie Till-Mobley in the 1950s, before the 14-year-old's 1955 murder in Mississippi became one of the defining moments of the civil rights movement. It was named a Chicago Landmark in 2021 on the application of the nonprofit Blacks in Green, which now runs it as the Till House Museum.
emmett-till-mamie-till-mobley-house.descriptor: West Woodlawn two-flat where Emmett Till lived, now the Till House Museum

ernest-hemingway-birthplace-museum.text: Ernest Hemingway was born in this Oak Park house on July 21, 1899. The Queen Anne was designed by architect Wesley Arnold and built in 1890 for his grandparents, and was the first home in Oak Park with electricity; the Ernest Hemingway Foundation of Oak Park bought it in 1992, restored it, and opened it to the public as a museum in 2001.
ernest-hemingway-birthplace-museum.descriptor: Queen Anne house at 339 N. Oak Park Ave. where Hemingway was born in 1899

ernie-banks.text: "Mr. Cub" spent all 19 of his big-league seasons with the Chicago Cubs (1953-1971), hit 512 home runs, won back-to-back MVPs in 1958 and 1959, and gave the city the line "It's a beautiful day for a ballgame... let's play two!" He died in January 2015 and is buried here at Graceland, not far from Wrigley Field.
ernie-banks.descriptor: Ernie Banks' grave in Graceland Cemetery, 4001 N Clark St

ever.text: Chef Curtis Duffy and partner Michael Muser opened Ever on Fulton Street in July 2020, after their previous restaurant, Grace, held three Michelin stars for four straight years before closing in December 2017. Ever has earned two Michelin stars of its own.
ever.descriptor: Curtis Duffy's two-Michelin-star tasting-menu restaurant on W. Fulton St

farm-in-the-zoo.text: Opened in 1964 and renovated in 2002, Farm-in-the-Zoo puts cattle, chickens, goats, pigs, rabbits and ponies in a set of real barns so city kids can see, hear and smell a working farm. Seasonal programs let visitors interact with and feed some of the animals, and like the rest of Lincoln Park Zoo, it's free.
farm-in-the-zoo.descriptor: Working-farm exhibit at free Lincoln Park Zoo, open since 1964

federales-logan-square.text: Federales opened at Milwaukee and Sacramento in September 2023 on part of the old Marcello's Father & Son site — the tavern-pizza institution that closed in 2019 after 72 years in Logan Square. It is the second Chicago outpost of the Four Corners taco-and-tequila bar: an 8,500-square-foot room, a patio with a retractable roof, and murals by Jason Botkin.
federales-logan-square.descriptor: Tequila and taco bar at Milwaukee & Sacramento with a retractable-roof patio

field-museum.text: Incorporated in 1893 as the Columbian Museum of Chicago to keep artifacts from the World's Columbian Exposition, it was renamed in 1905 for department-store magnate Marshall Field, its first major benefactor. It moved to the lakefront site in 1921 and now holds over 24 million specimens, including Sue, the largest T. rex found at the time of her 2000 debut.
field-museum.descriptor: Natural history museum on the Museum Campus, home to Sue the T. rex

frank-lloyd-wright-home-and-studio.text: Wright built the shingled house in 1889 and added the studio annex in 1898; across the two decades he worked here, he and his draftsmen turned out the Robie House, Unity Temple, the Larkin Building and the Dana-Thomas House. He left in 1909, and the complex has been a National Historic Landmark since 1976 — the Frank Lloyd Wright Preservation Trust runs guided tours today.
frank-lloyd-wright-home-and-studio.descriptor: Wright's own 1889 house and 1898 studio in Oak Park, now a house museum

writtenFor.name: Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio

frederick-c-robie-house.text: Frank Lloyd Wright designed it for manufacturing executive Frederick C. Robie and finished it in 1910 — the definitive Prairie-style house, with sweeping cantilevered roofs, an open plan and 175 art-glass panels in 29 patterns. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1963 and, in 2019, part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of eight Wright buildings.
frederick-c-robie-house.descriptor: Frank Lloyd Wright's 1910 Prairie-style landmark in Hyde Park

frontera-grill.text: Rick Bayless's first restaurant opened at 445 N. Clark on March 21, 1987, putting regional Mexican cooking on a serious American restaurant stage at a time when few kitchens did. In 2007 the James Beard Foundation named Frontera the Outstanding Restaurant in the United States.
frontera-grill.descriptor: Rick Bayless's regional Mexican restaurant on N. Clark, open since 1987

gale-street-inn.text: A Jefferson Park standby on Milwaukee Avenue that still bills itself as home to Chicago's finest ribs, where tender baked ribs and juicy barbecue chicken arrive as full-course dinners with bread, salad and sides like a cheesy twice-baked potato.
gale-street-inn.descriptor: Old-school Jefferson Park rib house at Milwaukee Ave and Gale St

gallager.text: This ordinary house on South Homan Avenue played the Gallagher family home on Showtime's Shameless, which ran from 2011 to 2021. The show is set in Back of the Yards, but North Lawndale was its primary Chicago filming location, and the real house has drawn fans who come to see it in person.
gallager.descriptor: North Lawndale house used as the Gallagher home exterior on TV's Shameless

gallagher-way.text: The plaza opened April 10, 2017 as "The Park at Wrigley," timed to the Cubs' home opener, and sits just outside Wrigley Field. Bronze statues of five Cubs legends stand in it — Ernie Banks, Billy Williams, Ron Santo, Ferguson Jenkins, and Ryne Sandberg, whose statue was unveiled on June 23, 2024, the 40th anniversary of "The Sandberg Game."
gallagher-way.descriptor: Public plaza outside Wrigley Field with five Cubs legend statues

garfield-park.text: Laid out in the 1870s by William Le Baron Jenney — the engineer later called the father of the skyscraper — it opened in 1874 as Central Park and was renamed in 1881 for the assassinated President James A. Garfield. Jens Jensen reshaped it as West Park System superintendent from 1905, adding the lagoon and designing the 4.5-acre conservatory, one of the largest plant conservatories in the country.
garfield-park.descriptor: 184-acre West Side park with a golden-domed fieldhouse and conservatory

garfield-park-conservatory.text: Jens Jensen designed it with Prairie School architects Schmidt, Garden and Martin, and it was built in 1906-07 as a series of naturalistic landscapes under glass rather than the usual rows of potted plants. A hailstorm on June 30, 2011 shattered much of the glass, and phased reopenings ran through January 2012. Admission is free for Chicago residents.
garfield-park-conservatory.descriptor: 1906-07 glasshouse on N Central Park Ave, "landscape art under glass"

gejas-cafe.text: A dim, candlelit Lincoln Park fondue room that has been a reliable special-occasion date restaurant for decades: cheese fondue, then meat and seafood cooked at the table, then flaming chocolate, with a classical and flamenco guitarist playing live among the tables.
gejas-cafe.descriptor: Candlelit Lincoln Park fondue restaurant with live flamenco guitar

gene-georgetti.text: Gene Michelotti and Alfredo Federighi, nicknamed "Georgetti" after a celebrated Italian cyclist, opened this Tuscan-Italian steakhouse in 1941, and it bills itself as Chicago's oldest steakhouse. The walls are hung with decades of signed celebrity photos and familiar local faces.
gene-georgetti.descriptor: River North steakhouse at 500 N Franklin St, open since 1941

getty-tomb.text: Lumber baron Henry Harrison Getty hired Louis Sullivan to design this tomb for his wife Carrie Eliza in 1890; it is often called the most significant piece of architecture in Graceland Cemetery and the start of Sullivan's work in the Chicago School. A plaster cast of its ornate bronze door won him an award at the 1900 Paris Exposition. Sullivan himself is buried in the same cemetery.
getty-tomb.descriptor: Louis Sullivan's 1890 limestone mausoleum in Graceland Cemetery

gibsons-bar-steakhouse.text: Gibsons opened on Rush Street in 1989 and was the founding restaurant of what is now Gibsons Restaurant Group. It has been called Chicago's top-grossing independent restaurant, and the group is unusual in holding its own USDA certification for its beef rather than buying to someone else's grade.
gibsons-bar-steakhouse.descriptor: Steakhouse on Rush Street in River North, open since 1989

ginos-east.text: Three cab drivers — Sam Levine, Fred Bartoli and George Loverde — opened Gino's East on E. Superior Street in 1966. In the 1970s customers started carving their initials into the tables, so the staff handed out markers and pointed them at the walls instead; graffiti now covers nearly every inch of the flagship. It left the address in 2000 and returned to a new building on the same spot in 2006.
ginos-east.descriptor: Deep-dish pizzeria off the Magnificent Mile with graffiti-covered walls, 1966

girl-the-goat.text: Stephanie Izard was the first woman to win Bravo's Top Chef, and in July 2010 she opened Girl & the Goat on West Randolph with Boka Restaurant Group. The menu is globally inflected shared plates with a nose-to-tail streak, including offal. It was a James Beard Best New Restaurant semifinalist in 2011, and Izard won the Beard award for Best Chef: Great Lakes in 2013.
girl-the-goat.descriptor: Stephanie Izard's shared-plates restaurant on W Randolph in the West Loop, since 2010

goodman-theatre-center.text: Founded in 1925 and named for playwright Kenneth Sawyer Goodman, who died in the 1918 flu pandemic, it was built with a $250,000 gift from his parents to the Art Institute of Chicago. The company won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 1992 and moved to its Dearborn Street home, with the Albert and Owen theaters, in 2000. Its annual "A Christmas Carol" is a Chicago holiday fixture.
goodman-theatre-center.descriptor: Chicago's oldest nonprofit theater, 170 N Dearborn in the Loop

goose-island-brewery.text: Goose Island began in 1988 as a brewpub in Chicago's Lincoln Park, named for a nearby island, and is the oldest currently operating brewing company in Illinois. A larger production brewery opened in 1995. It's the home of Bourbon County Stout, the bourbon-barrel-aged beer brewer Greg Hall created in the early 1990s.
goose-island-brewery.descriptor: Goose Island's Fulton Street production brewery, West Town

grant-park.text: Laid out as Lake Park in 1844 and renamed for Ulysses S. Grant in 1901, 'Chicago's front yard' stayed open lakefront largely because merchant Aaron Montgomery Ward fought four court battles to keep buildings out of it. Its 319 acres later hosted the 1968 Democratic convention clashes, Obama's 2008 election-night speech and Lollapalooza.
grant-park.descriptor: 319-acre lakefront park downtown, known as 'Chicago's front yard'

greek-islands.text: Greek Islands opened at 200 S. Halsted in 1971 and is one of the surviving Greektown tavernas: the Halsted restaurant row lost the Parthenon, Santorini and Pegasus in 2016 and the Pan Hellenic Pastry Shop in 2017. Flaming saganaki — the "Opa!" cheese dish now served all over the neighborhood — was invented a few doors away at the Parthenon.
greek-islands.descriptor: Greektown taverna on S. Halsted, open since 1971

green-mill-cocktail-lounge.text: The bar traces back to a roadhouse from about 1898 and became Green Mill Gardens in 1914, the name a nod to Paris's Moulin Rouge. During Prohibition, Al Capone gunman "Machine Gun" Jack McGurn was a part-owner, and the curved booth known as Capone's booth is still in the room. It has been a full-time jazz club since Dave Jemilo took over in 1986 — the same year the Uptown Poetry Slam started here.
green-mill-cocktail-lounge.descriptor: Uptown jazz club and former Prohibition speakeasy on N. Broadway

gwendolyn-brooks.text: Gwendolyn Brooks became the first African American to win a Pulitzer Prize when "Annie Allen" took the 1950 poetry award. She wrote Bronzeville from the inside — her breakthrough book was "A Street in Bronzeville" (1945) — and said of her corner apartment there: "I lived in a small second-floor apartment at the corner, and I could look first on one side and then the other. There was my material."
gwendolyn-brooks.descriptor: Memorial plaque to the Pulitzer-winning poet on 35th Street in Bronzeville

harold-washington.text: Harold Washington became Chicago's first Black mayor in 1983, spent his first term deadlocked against a 29-alderman council bloc in the fight known as Council Wars, won reelection in 1987 and then died of a heart attack that November, months into his second term. He is buried here at Oak Woods, the 1853 cemetery that also holds Ida B. Wells, Jesse Owens and Enrico Fermi.
harold-washington.descriptor: Harold Washington's grave in Oak Woods Cemetery, Greater Grand Crossing

harry-carays-italian-steakhouse.text: Cubs broadcaster Harry Caray lent his name to this 1987 steakhouse in the old Chicago Varnish Company building. In 2003 the restaurant group's Grant DePorter paid $113,824.16 for the Steve Bartman foul ball and had a special-effects expert publicly detonate it on February 26, 2004; fragments are still displayed at the restaurant, and in 2005 the group boiled the remains and worked the captured steam into a pasta sauce.
harry-carays-italian-steakhouse.descriptor: Steak and Italian-American in River North's old Chicago Varnish Co. building

hawthorne-race-course.text: Edward Corrigan, owner of 1890 Kentucky Derby winner Riley, established Hawthorne in Stickney, and it ran from 1891 under the Carey family for most of its life. It survived grandstand fires in 1902 and 1978 and a 1905 Chicago racing ban, but after its license was revoked in January 2026 and a February Chapter 11 filing, it ran its final race on July 19, 2026 and sold for $90 million to a buyer linked to data-center operator Digital Realty.
hawthorne-race-course.descriptor: Historic Stickney horse-racing track, 1891 to 2026, now closed

home-run-inn-pizzeria.text: Home Run Inn traces back to a 1923 tavern on 31st Street owned by Mary and Vincent Grittani, named after a home run from a nearby game came through the window. Mary worked out the thin-crust pizza recipe in the 1940s — still the one they use — and the company started selling frozen pies in the 1950s. Only four of its nine locations are inside the city.
home-run-inn-pizzeria.descriptor: Chicago thin-crust pizzeria on Archer Ave

writtenFor.name: Home Run Inn Pizzeria - South Lawndale

home-run-inn-pizzeria-south-lawndale.text: Home Run Inn traces back to a 1923 tavern on 31st Street that got its name after a ball from a nearby game came through the front window. Mary Grittani worked out the thin-crust pizza recipe in the 1940s — still the one they use — and the family started selling frozen pies in the 1950s. This Archer Avenue pizzeria is one of only a handful of locations inside the city.
home-run-inn-pizzeria-south-lawndale.descriptor: Chicago thin-crust pizzeria on Archer Ave in Garfield Ridge

writtenFor.name: Home Run Inn Pizzeria - Garfield Ridge

hopleaf-bar.text: Michael Roper opened Hopleaf on February 15, 1992 in the old Clark Foster Liquors space at 5148 N. Clark, turning a corner liquor store into one of Chicago's first serious Belgian and craft beer bars. The kitchen followed the beer list — mussels and frites are the house signature.
hopleaf-bar.descriptor: Belgian-style beer bar on N Clark St in Andersonville, open since 1992

hugos-frog-bar-fish-house.text: Hugo's has been serving oysters, Alaskan king crab and its namesake frog legs at 1024 N. Rush since 1997, sharing its building — and second-floor private dining rooms — with Gibsons Bar & Steakhouse. Both belong to Gibsons Restaurant Group, founded in 1989.
hugos-frog-bar-fish-house.descriptor: Gold Coast seafood and steak house on Rush Street known for frog legs

humboldt-alexander-von-park.text: Opened in 1877 and named for the German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, the 207-acre park got its prairie-style rework from Jens Jensen between 1905 and 1920 — the winding river, the rose garden, the boathouse and the field house are his. It is a center of Chicago's Puerto Rican community; the National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts and Culture opened in the restored stables and receptory building in 2009.
humboldt-alexander-von-park.descriptor: 207-acre West Side park with lagoons, boathouse and Jens Jensen landscaping

huntington-bank-pavilion-at-northerly-is.text: This lakefront amphitheater sits on the old runway of Meigs Field. On the night of March 30, 2003 Mayor Richard M. Daley sent crews out to bulldoze X-shaped gouges into the airstrip, stranding aircraft and drawing the FAA's maximum fine of $33,000; the island became parkland and the concert venue opened in 2005. It has since been the Charter One, FirstMerit and Huntington Bank pavilion.
huntington-bank-pavilion-at-northerly-is.descriptor: Seasonal lakefront amphitheater on Northerly Island, facing the skyline

writtenFor.name: Huntington Bank Pavilion at Northerly Island

indienne.text: Chef Sujan Sarkar opened Indienne in September 2022 in the old Graham Elliot space, and in 2023 it became the first Michelin-starred Indian restaurant in Chicago. Sarkar was a James Beard "Best Chef: Great Lakes" nominee in 2024, and the restaurant was named Restaurant of the Year at the 2026 Jean Banchet Awards.
indienne.descriptor: Progressive Indian fine dining at 217 W. Huron, River North

intelligentsia.text: Intelligentsia was founded in Chicago in 1995 by Doug Zell and Emily Mange and became a standard-bearer of American third-wave coffee, buying beans directly from growers in Central and South America and East Africa. In 2008 it stopped serving 20-ounce drinks, saying large sizes were "masking and adulterating" the flavors it worked to source and roast. This shop sits on Randolph across from Millennium Park.
intelligentsia.descriptor: Millennium Park coffeebar at 53 E. Randolph in the Loop

intelligentsia-coffee.text: Doug Zell and Emily Mange left San Francisco in search of freshly roasted coffee and opened Intelligentsia's first coffeebar and roastery in Lakeview on October 9, 1995, installing a Probat L12 and building the brand around Black Cat espresso. It went on to become one of the defining names in American third-wave coffee.
intelligentsia-coffee.descriptor: Third-wave coffeebar and roaster at 3123 N. Broadway in Lakeview

io-theater.text: Del Close and Charna Halpern founded ImprovOlympic in 1981, and its house long-form structure, the Harold, shaped generations of performers — Tina Fey, Amy Poehler, Stephen Colbert, Bill Hader and Seth Meyers all came up through it. iO closed in June 2020 under pandemic pressure, but new owners bought the Kingsbury Street complex in July 2021 and reopened it on November 3, 2022.
io-theater.descriptor: Improv theater at 1501 N. Kingsbury in Lincoln Park

italian-village.text: Alfredo Capitanini, a Tuscan immigrant who reached Chicago in 1924, opened The Village in 1927, and his family still runs it. The Monroe Street building has since grown into several restaurants stacked under one roof: The Village on the second floor for family-style Italian-American, Vivere on the first floor, and Sotto with its bar in the lower level.
italian-village.descriptor: Loop Italian restaurant complex on W Monroe, family-run since 1927

james-m-nederlander-theatre.text: Rapp & Rapp built this 1926 movie palace as the Oriental, piling India-inspired ornament into a Loop lot with a grim past: it stands on the site of the 1903 Iroquois Theatre fire, the deadliest single-building fire in U.S. history. It closed as a movie house in 1981, sat vacant for over a decade, reopened for live theater in 1998, ran Wicked from 2005 to 2009, and was renamed for impresario James M. Nederlander in 2019.
james-m-nederlander-theatre.descriptor: Loop Broadway house at 24 W Randolph, opened 1926 as the Oriental Theatre

james-r-thompson.text: The white memorial marks the corner where James Richard Thompson, a 26-year-old from Plainfield, was struck and killed while crossing around 1 a.m. on a Saturday in March 2023. Police said the driver ran a stop sign and fled east on Washington Boulevard; his family called him "a shining light that brought joy and happiness everywhere he went."
james-r-thompson.descriptor: Roadside ghost-bike memorial at Washington and Green in the West Loop

jane-addams-hull-house-museum.text: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull House here in 1889 as a settlement house for the immigrant Near West Side. It grew to 13 buildings by 1911 and drove Progressive-era reforms on child labor and the first juvenile court in the United States. Most of the complex was razed for UIC in the 1960s; the original 1856 mansion survives as a free museum.
jane-addams-hull-house-museum.descriptor: Free museum in the 1856 Hull mansion on S Halsted, on the UIC campus

jay-pritzker-pavilion.text: Frank Gehry's billowing stainless-steel bandshell opened in July 2004 and holds 11,000 between fixed seats and the Great Lawn. The steel trellis arcing overhead is not decoration — it carries a distributed sound system designed to mimic indoor concert-hall acoustics. To get around Grant Park's historic height limits, the city classifies the structure as a work of art rather than a building.
jay-pritzker-pavilion.descriptor: Frank Gehry bandshell in Millennium Park; free Grant Park Music Festival

jerk-taco-man-greater-grand-crossing.text: Julius Thomas sold jerk tacos out of the back of his wife's hair salon near Pulaski and Wilcox before opening a Garfield Park storefront in 2014, then adding this 12,000-square-foot South Side restaurant on State Street in 2016. Beyond the jerk there is red snapper, curry goat, oxtail stew and 18-hour smoked brisket. "I'm not cheap with the spices and I'm not cheap with the meat," he told Block Club Chicago.
jerk-taco-man-greater-grand-crossing.descriptor: Jamaican jerk and taco restaurant on S State St, Greater Grand Crossing

writtenFor.name: Jerk Taco Man - Greater Grand Crossing

jimmys-red-hots.text: A purist stand at Grand and Pulaski known for the Depression Dog: a steamed natural-casing Vienna Beef frank served with a handful of hand-cut fries piled in the wrapper, no tomato and absolutely no ketchup. There's no seating and nothing char-grilled — just dogs, Polish sausage, tamales and a housemade habanero sauce.
jimmys-red-hots.descriptor: Humboldt Park hot dog stand at Grand & Pulaski — Depression dogs, no ketchup

jims-original.text: Jimmy Stefanovic, a Macedonian immigrant, took over his aunt and uncle's hot dog stand at Maxwell and Halsted in 1939, and the stand is credited with the Maxwell Street Polish — grilled sausage, grilled onions, yellow mustard and sport peppers on a bun. When UIC's South Campus expansion razed the old market district, Jim's and its longtime neighbor Express Grill both moved to Union Avenue.
jims-original.descriptor: Late-night Maxwell Street Polish stand at Union & Roosevelt, since 1939

jims-original-little-italy.text: Jim's Original began in 1939 when Macedonian immigrant Jimmy Stefanovic took over his aunt and uncle's hot dog stand at Maxwell and Halsted, and the Maxwell Street Polish — grilled sausage buried in sweet onions and mustard — is widely credited to him. When UIC's campus expansion demolished the old Maxwell Street market in 2005, Jim's relocated to Union Avenue; this outpost serves the same menu.
jims-original-little-italy.descriptor: Chicago stand serving the Maxwell Street Polish, from the 1939 original

joan-w-and-irving-b-harris-theater-for-m.text: Opened in 2003 and named for donors Joan and Irving Harris, the Harris is built largely underground — Grant Park height restrictions meant burying the hall and leaving only a glass-walled lobby above Randolph Street. It gave mid-sized companies like the Joffrey Ballet, Hubbard Street Dance Chicago and Chicago Opera Theater a stage they had long lacked.
joan-w-and-irving-b-harris-theater-for-m.descriptor: 1,499-seat music and dance hall on the north edge of Millennium Park

writtenFor.name: Joan W. and Irving B. Harris Theater for Music and Dance

joes-on-weed-st.text: Joe's has been on Weed Street since 1997 — a 20,000-square-foot warehouse-style venue with seven party rooms and more than 100 TVs that doubles as Chicago's Nashville outpost. It is an eight-time winner of the Academy of Country Music's Nightclub/Club of the Year award.
joes-on-weed-st.descriptor: 20,000-sq-ft warehouse country-music and sports bar on Weed St since 1997

joes-seafood-prime-steak-stone-crab.text: This is the Chicago branch of Joe's Stone Crab, the Miami Beach institution Joe and Jenny Weiss opened in 1913 on the strength of a dish Joe first dismissed when a scientist suggested it — stone crab claws. Lettuce Entertain You opened this River North version in 1999, the first branch outside Miami Beach; Las Vegas (2005) and Washington, D.C. (2014) followed.
joes-seafood-prime-steak-stone-crab.descriptor: Steak and stone crab house on E. Grand in River North since 1999

writtenFor.name: Joe's Seafood, Prime Steak & Stone Crab

kamehachi.text: Marion Konishi opened Kamehachi in 1967 in its Old Town spot across from Second City, and it bills itself as Chicago's first sushi restaurant. It's still family-run, now by her daughter and granddaughter.
kamehachi.descriptor: Old Town sushi bar at 1531 N Wells St, open since 1967

kanela-breakfast-club.text: Kanela — Greek for cinnamon — started in Lakeview in 2010 and grew into a small Chicago group of breakfast-and-lunch rooms, now four locations including this Streeterville one. The menu is classic American breakfast bent by Greek influence, with the namesake spice turning up throughout.
kanela-breakfast-club.descriptor: Greek-inflected breakfast and brunch spot on E Illinois St in Streeterville

kasama.text: Husband-and-wife chefs Tim Flores and Genie Kwon opened Kasama in July 2020 as a casual spot for pastries and lumpia; the pandemic pushed them into a multi-course dinner tasting menu, and in 2022 it became the first Filipino restaurant anywhere in the world to earn a Michelin star. The name is Tagalog for "together."
kasama.descriptor: Filipino bakery by day, tasting-menu restaurant by night, Ukrainian Village

kenneth-c-griffin-museum-of-science-and-.text: The building is the surviving Palace of Fine Arts from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the one fair hall given a permanent brick substructure beneath its plaster facade. It opened as a museum in stages beginning in 1933, funded by Sears president Julius Rosenwald, and holds the captured German submarine U-505, the Pioneer Zephyr, the Apollo 8 command module and a full-size coal mine. It was renamed in 2024 after Ken Griffin's $125 million gift.
kenneth-c-griffin-museum-of-science-and-.descriptor: Science museum in Jackson Park's 1893 World's Fair Palace of Fine Arts

writtenFor.name: Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry

kingston-mines.text: Open since 1968 and billed as Chicago's oldest continuously operating blues club, Kingston Mines takes its name from the Kingston Mines Theatre Company, which premiered "Grease" in 1971 before it went to Broadway. Owner Doc Pellegrino ran two stages so one band starts the moment the other finishes and the music never stops. Koko Taylor and Magic Slim played here; the Rolling Stones turned up in 1978.
kingston-mines.descriptor: Late-night Lincoln Park blues club with two alternating stages

kitty-osheas.text: The pub sits in the Hilton Chicago, which opened in 1927 as the Stevens Hotel and was then the largest hotel in the world. Inside it's dark wood, fish-and-chips and corned beef.
kitty-osheas.descriptor: Irish pub inside the Hilton Chicago at 720 S Michigan Ave

kumas-corner-belmont.text: Kuma's Corner opened in Avondale in 2005 with a heavy-metal theme, and is credited with helping popularize the pretzel bun. Its Ghost Burger, topped with an unconsecrated communion wafer, drew boycott calls from the Archdiocese of Chicago in 2013 and was later named by TIME one of the most influential burgers of all time.
kumas-corner-belmont.descriptor: Heavy-metal burger bar on W. Belmont in Avondale since 2005

kumiko.text: Julia Momosé opened Kumiko on New Year's Eve 2018; the name comes from the Japanese woodworking craft of fitting delicate pieces into patterns without nails or fasteners. The bar treats its drink list and its kitchen as equals, and it won the James Beard Award for Outstanding Bar in 2025 after repeated appearances on the World's 50 Best Bars list.
kumiko.descriptor: Julia Momosé's Japanese cocktail and dining bar on W Lake St, West Loop

la-pasadita.text: La Pasadita ran two storefronts on the same East Village block of Ashland, both turning out the same thing to the same standard: plain tacos of meat, chopped onion and cilantro that Time Out rated among the best in the city.
la-pasadita.descriptor: No-frills taqueria at 1140 N Ashland Ave in East Village

lao-sze-chuan.text: Chef Tony Hu, a Sichuan native, opened the first Lao Sze Chuan at 2172 S Archer Ave in 1998, and the Chicago Tribune gave it a three-fork rating in 1999 — a rare nod for a Chinese restaurant at the time. It landed on Michelin's Bib Gourmand list seven times between 2010 and 2016 and grew into a multi-location group.
lao-sze-chuan.descriptor: Sichuan restaurant on S Archer Ave in Chinatown, open since 1998

le-bouchon.text: One of Chicago's longest-running French bistros, open in Bucktown since 1993 and still packed into a small, crowded room Time Out calls the closest thing Chicago has to a little Paris bistro. The orders that never change: the caramelized onion tart, onion soup under a gluttonous lid of Gruyère, steak frites, and duck for two.
le-bouchon.descriptor: French bistro at 1958 N Damen Ave in Bucktown since 1993

le-colonial.text: Vietnamese cooking under French-colonial influence, served in palm-filled rooms with a dim upstairs lounge and a year-round terrace over Oak Street; the kitchen is known for crispy shrimp beignets and ginger-marinated duck. The Chicago dining room is one of a small group with siblings in New York, Houston, Atlanta and four other cities.
le-colonial.descriptor: French-Vietnamese fine dining with an Oak Street terrace in the Gold Coast

leaning-tower-of-niles.text: Industrialist Robert Ilg had this half-scale copy of the Leaning Tower of Pisa built in 1934 — designed by architect Albert L. Farr — to hide the water tank and pumping equipment for the pools and artificial lake at his employees' recreation park. Niles became a sister city of Pisa in 1991, the village bought the tower from the YMCA for $10 in 2015, and it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2020.
leaning-tower-of-niles.descriptor: Half-size 1934 replica of the Leaning Tower of Pisa in suburban Niles

lems-bar-b-q.text: The Lemons brothers left Indianola, Mississippi for Chicago in 1948 and opened Lem's in 1954 — part of the Great Migration wave that turned South Side barbecue into its own tradition. Ribs go into a glass-fronted aquarium smoker and finish over hickory, and the rib tips added in 1968 are the order to place. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2025.
lems-bar-b-q.descriptor: Chatham rib-tip and hot-link joint on E. 75th St, founded 1954

leonas.text: Leona's started in 1950 as a single Lakeview storefront and grew into one of Chicago's best-known family pizza names, serving thin crust, deep dish, Sicilian and pan pizza alongside Italian beef, pasta and fried mozzarella bricks. Three Chicago-area locations remain, including this one on Irving Park Road.
leonas.descriptor: Italian-American pizzeria at 4363 W Irving Park Rd; founded 1950

lillies-q.text: Chef Charlie McKenna opened Lillie's Q in 2010, naming it for his grandmother Lillie — born in 1927 in Beaufort, South Carolina, and known in the family for her barbecue — and the "Q" for his father, Quito. A competition pitmaster, McKenna smokes low and slow over peach wood and leans Carolina, with a vinegar-based Carolina sauce among the housemade sauces on the table.
lillies-q.descriptor: Carolina-leaning barbecue from a competition pitmaster, smoked over peach wood

lincoln-abraham-park.text: At roughly 1,200 acres running seven miles up the North Side lakefront, this is Chicago's largest park and the second-most-visited city park in the country after Central Park. It began as the municipal burial ground in 1843; the city converted it to parkland by 1864, relocating an estimated 35,000 bodies, and renamed it in June 1865 for the newly assassinated Abraham Lincoln. Lincoln Park Zoo inside is still free.
lincoln-abraham-park.descriptor: Chicago's largest park, seven miles of lakefront with a free zoo

lincoln-hall.text: The building opened in 1912 as the Fullerton Theatre and spent 1964 to 2006 as the 3-Penny Cinema, known for second-run and midnight movies. Chris and Mike Schuba converted it into Lincoln Hall, a 507-capacity music venue, in October 2009, then sold it and sister club Schubas Tavern to Audiotree in 2015.
lincoln-hall.descriptor: 507-capacity rock club on N Lincoln Ave in Lincoln Park, in a 1912 theater

lincoln-park-conservatory-garden.text: The conservatory's ogee-arched glass houses went up between 1890 and 1895 to designs by Joseph Lyman Silsbee and Mifflin E. Bell, and a fiddle-leaf rubber tree about 50 feet tall still towers inside the Palm House, which opened in 1892. The Great Garden outside is older than the building — laid out in the late 1870s around the Eli Bates Fountain and the Schiller monument. Admission is free.
lincoln-park-conservatory-garden.descriptor: Free Victorian glasshouse and garden at 2391 N Stockton Dr, Lincoln Park

lincoln-park-zoo.text: Founded in 1868 with a gift of swans from New York's Central Park, Lincoln Park Zoo is one of the oldest zoos in North America and one of the last big ones you can still walk into for free, open 365 days a year. Its most famous resident was Bushman, a lowland gorilla who drew crowds from 1931 until his death in 1951.
lincoln-park-zoo.descriptor: Free 1868 zoo in Lincoln Park, one of the oldest in North America

little-goat-diner.text: Top Chef winner Stephanie Izard opened Little Goat in 2012 as the casual counterpart to her West Loop hit Girl & the Goat — an upscale diner built around all-day breakfast and an expanded version of her bread program. It moved north to Lakeview's Southport corridor in April 2023, still turning out pancakes, burgers, waffles and house ice cream.
little-goat-diner.descriptor: Stephanie Izard's all-day diner on the Southport corridor in Lakeview

logan-square.text: This green circle is the grand northwest terminus of Chicago's boulevard system, designed by William Le Baron Jenney and landscape architect Jens Jensen among others. At its center is the Illinois Centennial Monument, a 70-foot Tennessee marble Doric column topped by an eagle, raised in 1918 for the state's hundredth birthday and designed by Henry Bacon, the architect of the Lincoln Memorial.
logan-square.descriptor: Boulevard-system plaza with the 1918 Illinois Centennial Monument

longman-eagle.text: Longman & Eagle opened in Logan Square in 2010 as a modern take on the old Chicago inn — eat, drink and sleep in one building, with six guest rooms above the dining room and a deep whiskey list. It held a Michelin star from 2011 through 2017, then moved onto the guide's Bib Gourmand list, where it has stayed.
longman-eagle.descriptor: Logan Square gastropub and whiskey bar on N Kedzie with a six-room inn upstairs

lotties-pub.text: Walter "Lottie" Zagorski took over the storefront in 1934 and turned it into a tavern — a flamboyant barkeep who ran an underground gambling room in the basement with horse betting, all-night poker and strip acts, drawing gangsters and politicians. Lottie died in 1973 and a federal crackdown shut the place in 1974; a new owner revived the name in 1986 as the sports bar it is today.
lotties-pub.descriptor: Bucktown sports bar on Cortland St, a tavern on this corner since 1934

lou-malnatis-pizzeria.text: Lou Malnati learned deep dish from the ground up: his father Rudy was making it in the 1940s and Lou co-managed Pizzeria Uno in the 1950s. Lou and his wife Jean opened the first Malnati's in suburban Lincolnwood on St. Patrick's Day 1971; after Lou died in 1978, Jean and sons Marc and Rick kept it going, and the family name is now the city's best-known deep-dish brand.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish pizzeria at 439 N. Wells St. in River North

writtenFor.name: Lou Malnati's Pizzeria - River North (North Wells Street)

lou-malnatis-pizzeria-chicago-loop.text: Lou Malnati grew up in the deep-dish trade — his father Rudy co-managed Pizzeria Uno, where the Chicago-style pie was born — and Lou opened his own pizzeria with his wife Jean in Lincolnwood in 1971. It has since grown past 60 Chicagoland locations, and Yelp named it America's top pizza chain of its size in 2025.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria-chicago-loop.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish pizzeria, branch of the chain founded in 1971

lou-malnatis-pizzeria-clearing.text: Lou Malnati opened the first Lou Malnati's in Lincolnwood on St. Patrick's Day 1971, after learning deep dish alongside his father Rudy in the 1940s and co-managing Pizzeria Uno in the 1950s. His wife Jean and their sons took over when he died in 1978, and the family chain now runs more than 60 Chicagoland pizzerias — this one out on Cicero Avenue by Midway Airport.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria-clearing.descriptor: Deep-dish pizzeria on S Cicero Ave near Midway Airport

lou-malnatis-pizzeria-north-lincoln-aven.text: Lou Malnati opened the first Lou Malnati's in Lincolnwood on St. Patrick's Day 1971, after learning deep dish alongside his father Rudy in the 1940s and co-managing Pizzeria Uno in the 1950s. The family kept it going after he died in 1978 and now runs 60-plus Chicagoland locations — this one on Randolph Street, in the middle of the West Loop restaurant row.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria-north-lincoln-aven.descriptor: Deep-dish pizzeria on Randolph Street's West Loop restaurant row

writtenFor.name: Lou Malnati's Pizzeria - Fulton Market District

lou-malnatis-pizzeria-river-north.text: Lou Malnati grew up inside the deep-dish origin story: he and his father Rudy were making deep-dish at Pizzeria Uno from the 1940s, and the two co-managed it in the '50s before Lou and his wife Jean opened their own place in Lincolnwood on St. Patrick's Day, 1971. Lou died in 1978 and Jean and sons Marc and Rick kept it going — there are now 60-plus Chicagoland locations, of which this is one.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria-river-north.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish pizzeria near Rush and Division in the Gold Coast

lou-malnatis-pizzeria-river-north-north-.text: Lou Malnati learned deep dish working alongside his father Rudy, who co-managed Pizzeria Uno in the 1950s, then opened his own pizzeria with his wife Jean in suburban Lincolnwood on St. Patrick's Day 1971. The flaky buttercrust and edge-to-edge sausage patty from that first shop are still the house signature at this River North branch and dozens of others.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria-river-north-north-.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish with a buttercrust and sausage patty, at 439 N. Wells St.

lou-malnatis-pizzeria-rush-division.text: This is the first Lou Malnati's, opened March 17, 1971 by Lou and Jean Malnati — an Italian opening a pizzeria in a Jewish neighborhood on an Irish holiday, as the family tells it, and on opening day a car crashed through the dining room wall. Lou learned deep dish from his father Rudy in the 1940s, and the two later co-managed Pizzeria Uno in the 1950s; after Lou's death in 1978, Jean and sons Marc and Rick grew it into a chain.
lou-malnatis-pizzeria-rush-division.descriptor: The original Lou Malnati's, deep dish in Lincolnwood since 1971

writtenFor.name: Lou Malnati's Pizzeria - North Lincoln Avenue

lou-mitchells-restaurant.text: Open since 1923 on West Jackson near Union Station, Lou Mitchell's sits at the start of Route 66 and has been feeding travelers heading west ever since — the nationwide Route 66 restoration push was launched here in 2002. Since 1958 the staff has handed out free doughnut holes and Milk Duds while you wait, a Greek-hospitality habit of giving guests something sweet on arrival. It joined the National Register in 2006.
lou-mitchells-restaurant.descriptor: 1923 diner near Union Station billed as the first stop on Route 66

lula-cafe.text: Jason Hammel and Amalea Tshilds opened Lula Cafe on September 2, 1999 in a small Kedzie Boulevard storefront with a four-burner home stove and a dented set of thrifted pots and pans. It now spans three storefronts, Hammel has three James Beard Best Chef: Great Lakes nominations, and the brunch is what locals queue for.
lula-cafe.descriptor: Seasonal market-driven cafe on N Kedzie Blvd in Logan Square since 1999

lurie-garden.text: Opened in July 2004, Lurie Garden is Millennium Park's answer to Chicago's motto Urbs in Horto, "city in a garden." Dutch plantsman Piet Oudolf and landscape architects GGN filled it with about 35,000 perennials, roughly 60% of them Illinois natives. A 15-foot "Shoulder Hedge" keeps crowds leaving the Pritzker Pavilion from trampling it, and a diagonal boardwalk called the Seam traces the old Lake Michigan seawall.
lurie-garden.descriptor: 2.5-acre prairie-style perennial garden inside Millennium Park

maggie-daley-park.text: Opened in December 2014, the 20-acre Michael Van Valkenburgh design replaced the old Daley Bicentennial Plaza and is named for Maggie Daley, the city's former first lady, who died of cancer in 2011. Its quarter-mile ice-skating ribbon loops past rock-climbing walls and a three-acre children's Play Garden; the BP Pedestrian Bridge links it back to Millennium Park.
maggie-daley-park.descriptor: 20-acre lakefront park with an ice-skating ribbon and climbing walls

mannys-cafeteria-and-delicatessen.text: Manny's dates to 1942, when brothers Jack and Charlie Raskin opened a deli on the Near West Side. After the war Jack bought a place called Sunny's and renamed it for his son Emanuel — a two-letter change that spared him a whole new sign. The deli moved to South Jefferson Street in 1964 and is still run by the Raskins, and its cafeteria tray line has long been an informal clubhouse for Chicago politicians, Barack Obama among them.
mannys-cafeteria-and-delicatessen.descriptor: Jewish-style cafeteria deli at 1141 S. Jefferson St., open since 1942

maple-ash.text: Two-Michelin-star chef Danny Grant built this Gold Coast steakhouse around live fire — the steaks and even the seafood tower come off a wood-burning hearth. Its signature order is the bluntly named "I Don't Give a F*@k" menu, four courses picked entirely by the kitchen. The wine list has taken Wine Spectator's America's Best Wine Program award.
maple-ash.descriptor: Wood-fired Gold Coast steakhouse on W Maple St

marina-city.text: Bertrand Goldberg designed the two round 587-foot towers in 1959 and they went up between 1961 and 1968, at the time both the tallest residential buildings and the tallest reinforced-concrete structures in the world. Locals call them the corncobs; Wilco fans call them the Wilco Towers, after the cover of Yankee Hotel Foxtrot.
marina-city.descriptor: Bertrand Goldberg's 1960s "corncob" twin towers on the Chicago River

marios-italian-lemonade.text: Mario's has been scooping Italian lemonade, shaved ice shot through with lemon rind and zest, from a walk-up window on Taylor Street since 1954. It's open only for the warm months, roughly May into September, and the line down the sidewalk on a hot night is part of the ritual. Flavors run from cantaloupe with real melon chunks to chocolate and piña colada.
marios-italian-lemonade.descriptor: Seasonal Italian ice stand at 1068 W. Taylor St. in Little Italy since 1954

marshall-field.text: The department-store magnate's 1906 memorial pairs the two men who would later create the Lincoln Memorial: architect Henry Bacon and sculptor Daniel Chester French, whose seated bronze figure here is titled "Memory." Field is in good company at Graceland, where Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham, Potter Palmer and Philip Armour are also buried.
marshall-field.descriptor: Marshall Field's tomb in Graceland Cemetery, with the "Memory" statue
